doc.title: Bob Haggart interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 22, 1995

title: World's Greatest Jazz Band tours and European audiences
summary: Trips to Europe with changing personnel; encores and record-collecting fans such as those who knew Jerry Jerome.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah, it makes plenty of sense. Tell us about some of your time in Europe with what was called The World’s Greatest Jazz Band.

Milton. We did quite a few trips with the World’s Greatest Jazz Band. And I’ve been over since then too with a lot of the same guys, Kenny Davern and Yank Lawson and George Masso, and Ralph Sutton, and Jake Hanna. But we’ve been over every times it seems it’s a slightly different group. You hardly ever go over with exactly the same personnel. It’s little changes here and there for one reason or another. But the Germans © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

really seem to love jazz. They won’t let you off the stage, you’ve got to play two encores anyway at the end of a set, and sometimes three, and they get their feet stomping. Clap- stomp at the same time, and that means get ready to play another one. But you’ve got to pretend. You walk off the stage and you wait out there and then say, “Guess we’re going to do another one,” and start ambling back on again. You play a second one, and it starts over again. They don’t do that over here. I mean there’s something about Europe, it’s not just Germany, I mean they do the same thing I think in Scotland and in Scandinavia, in Stockholm.
Do you feel the appreciation is greater, and if so why?

I guess it’s because they’ve gotten it through just recordings. And when you come over in person they’re very thrilled. And they have all these records and they want you to autograph the records and they come in with a pile of records like that, and a lot of this stuff came out in Europe and you didn’t even know they existed. Of course you never see any royalties, that’s for sure. Things come out. So you sign a whole bunch of these things and it’s really an ego trip because you didn’t realize that people cared, you know? But over there they seem to. You feel like you’re a hero when you go over there. Now like Jerry Jerome has never been over there, and there’s a guy who’s made records with Glenn Miller and Benny Goodman, and Artie Shaw. And he’s never been to Europe. He went over for the first time to Holland and found out all these people knew who Jerry Jerome was because they were avid record collectors, you know? They don’t miss a thing. You certainly don’t see much of that over here.
